etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French infect, from Latin infectus, perfect passive participle of inficiō (“dye, taint”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To bring (the body or part of it) into contact with a substance that causes illness (a pathogen), so that the pathogen begins to act on the body; (of a pathogen) to come into contact with (a body or body part) and begin to act on it.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, Katie L. Burke, “In the News”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3, page 193:
quote.text: Bats host many high-profile viruses that can infect humans, including severe acute respiratory syndrome and Ebola.

quote.citation: 2020 February 18, Isabella Kwai, “How a Pharmacy Handles Mask Hoarders and Coronavirus Fears”, in The New York Times‎[1], →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 2020-02-18, Asia Pacific‎[2]:
quote.text: Ms. Tang’s inevitable contact with people who are ill has started to worry her. It did not help when she learned that someone living in a building near her own, in Siu Sai Wan, had been infected by the virus.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To contaminate (an object or substance) with a pathogen.
(transitive) To make somebody enthusiastic about one's own passion, or to communicate a feeling to others, or a feeling communicating itself to others.

quote.citation: 1834, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter XIII, in Francesca Carrara. […], volume II, London: Richard Bentley, […], (successor to Henry Colburn), →OCLC, page 164:
quote.text: Guido, by way of diverting the embarrassment which seemed to infect them all, began to unfasten the packet of letters.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii], line 187:
quote.text: And in the imitation of these twain, / Who, as Ulysses says, opinion crowns / With an imperial voice, many are infect.
